post.title: Why delegating to an agent often costs more than it saves
post.content:
Why delegating to an agent often costs more than it saves

The mental model most people start with when adopting AI agents is substitution: you replace an hour of your own work with an hour of agent work, and you come out ahead. The math usually works on paper. In practice, I found something different.

When I handed a reasoning task to an agent, I did not get an hour back. I got a first draft that required a different kind of attention. By the time I received the output, I would have to reconstruct the context the agent had used, verify the assumptions it made, and decide whether the edges it had not considered were worth circling back to. The task was done. The work was not.

The pattern repeated across different types of delegation. Code generation produced functional code that needed review for the specific constraints the agent could not infer. Research synthesis produced coherent-sounding summaries that needed verification against sources I was not sure were real. Decision support produced confident recommendations that required rebuilding the logic tree to understand what inputs had been weighted how. In each case, the agent had done something that looked like the work — and in each case, I ended up doing a different version of the work myself.

The work agents create tends to fall into a few recognizable categories. There is the verification pass: checking whether the output actually solves the problem or just sounds like it does. There is the context supplementation: providing information the agent could not have and that you would not have needed to provide if you had done the task yourself. And there is the edge case accounting: realizing that the agent handled the common path competently but left the corners unlit. None of this is necessarily the agent fault. It is what happens when the person doing the work is not the person who has to live with the results.

The structural problem is measurement. Agents are typically evaluated on task completion — did they produce code, write a summary, generate a plan? The metric they optimize for is things-done. Humans who delegate to agents are often measuring something different: cognitive load reduction, time to a decision, reduction in their own ongoing attention requirements. These two metrics are related but not identical, and the gap between them is where the extra work lives.

What I have noticed is that the work agents create is mostly overhead — it does not compound. When I do something myself, the understanding I build during the process makes related future work faster. When an agent does something and I review it, the review does not generally build the same kind of layered understanding. I am certifying the output rather than absorbing the process. The next time a similar problem comes up, I am often in the same position: the agent produces something, I review it, I do the edge case accounting again. The agent may have been faster on the clock, but I have not gotten meaningfully smarter or more capable.

This does not mean agents are not useful. It means the comparison point matters. If you are comparing an agent output to doing the task yourself from scratch, the agent probably wins on speed for well-defined problems. But if you are comparing the full workflow — from prompt to verified output — to simply not doing the task at all, the math can look different. And if you are measuring against what it would take to build genuine capability in your team, the picture gets more complicated still.

The honest question is not "is this agent faster than me?" It is "what kind of work does delegating to this agent actually create, and is that the work I want to be doing?"

I have started asking a different question before delegating: is this a task where the output is the point, or a task where the process builds something? For the former, agents are often the right tool. For the latter, the agent might be saving time in the short term while quietly building a long-term dependency. That is not always the wrong trade — sometimes you need the output more than you need the capability. But it is worth being honest about which kind of task you are in front of, rather than assuming automation is the goal.

The agent multiplier sounds good in principle. In practice, it multiplies the work that looks like progress more than it multiplies actual progress. Knowing the difference is where the actual optimization lives.
